## Series Overview

A wafer stage vibrates. A die heats up a few microns off its nominal position between one
inspection frame and the next. A part gets re-fixtured slightly rotated. None of that is a defect
-- it's just the image having moved -- but every downstream step (die-to-die comparison,
overlay metrology, a defect detector trained on a fixed coordinate frame) assumes the image
*hasn't* moved. **Image registration** is the fix: finding the transform that maps a drifted
image back onto a reference frame so the two line up pixel-for-pixel again.

This series builds a small, fully-controlled synthetic benchmark -- a golden "die image" plus two
known-drift scenarios (pure rigid/affine stage drift, and affine drift plus a smooth local elastic
warp standing in for thermal drift) -- specifically so every method below can be scored against
ground truth in pixels, not eyeballed from an overlay. Every method runs on the *same* pair, with
real code, so the comparison is apples-to-apples. Same ethos as the rest of this blog: real code,
real captured numbers, honest limitations reported alongside anything that works -- including a
phase-correlation failure mode that turned out to be a genuinely useful lesson about periodic
industrial patterns.

The last post in the series is the one that prompted the whole series: **which of these methods
are actually licensed for company (not just research) use** -- because a permissive code license
and a permissive pretrained-weights license are two different questions, and popular papers
(SuperGlue/SuperPoint) are a real trap here.

### Posts in this series

1. **Part 1** -- [The Benchmark and Classical Methods](01-classical-methods.qmd). Builds the
   synthetic die-image benchmark with known ground-truth drift, then runs phase correlation, ECC,
   and SIFT+RANSAC against it -- including an honest, explained failure: phase correlation gets
   confused by the image's own periodic grid pattern.
2. **Part 2** -- [Deep Learning: Affine Regression and Deep Feature Matching](02-dl-affine-and-feature-matching.qmd).
   A from-scratch CNN trained unsupervised to regress an affine transform, and LoFTR (a
   transformer-based deep feature matcher) as the commercially-licensed alternative to
   SuperGlue/SuperPoint -- with a genuinely surprising result about which one actually wins.
3. **Part 3** -- [Deep Learning: Deformable Registration](03-dl-deformable-registration.qmd). A
   from-scratch VoxelMorph-style network (U-Net + spatial transformer, trained unsupervised on a
   similarity + smoothness loss) -- the only method in the series that can actually correct the
   non-rigid "thermal drift" scenario, since every affine-only method above hits a hard floor
   there by construction.
4. **Part 4** -- [Head-to-Head, Licensing, and the Recommendation](04-comparison-licensing-recommendation.qmd).
   Every method's measured accuracy side by side, a license table (code license *and* pretrained-
   weights license, checked separately), and a concrete recommendation for semiconductor
   inspection work.
